list-item.p: Earlier steroid intervention and anakinra use in axi-cel toxicity management for LBCL in the third-line setting reduced CRS and ICANS duration.
No differences in toxicity rate/severity, overall/progression-free survival, cumulative steroid dose, or health care utilization were detected.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel) is an effective chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy for relapsed or refractory (R/R) large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL). However, controlling cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell–associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) without compromising therapeutic efficacy remains a difficult challenge. In July 2020, our center adopted a toxicity management protocol modified from cohort 4 of the registrational ZUMA-1 trial, with earlier steroid use and incorporation of anakinra. To evaluate this change, we conducted a retrospective analysis of patients receiving axi-cel for R/R LBCL in the third-line setting from January 2018 through April 2023. The outcomes of interest were toxicity incidence/duration, treatment response, CAR-T expansion, and drug/health care utilization. Of the 195 identified patients, the postchange cohort (n = 103) had higher rates of anakinra (22% vs 5%) and steroid use (88% vs 71%) use than the comparator cohort (n = 92), without increases in cumulative steroid dose. Overall CRS and ICANS rates were similar, with directionally lower severe (grade 3+) ICANS rates in the postchange cohort. A significant reduction in CRS and ICANS duration was observed with the new protocol (adjusted estimate, ˗0.93 days [95% confidence interval (CI), ˗1.67 to ˗0.19] and ˗2.49 days [95% CI, ˗4.96 to ˗0.03], respectively). Day 7 CAR-T expansion was lower in the postchange cohort, possibly due to earlier steroid use. However, efficacy outcomes, intensive care unit admission rates, and hospitalization length were similar between the cohorts. This study supports earlier intervention for CAR-T toxicities and establishes anakinra as a safe and effective alternative toxicity management drug to tocilizumab.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: CD19-directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell (CAR-T) therapy is an effective treatment for relapsed or refractory (R/R) large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL).1, 2, 3 ZUMA-1, the registration trial of axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel), showed an objective response rate of 82%, with a complete response (CR) rate (CRR) of 54%.1 Despite its efficacy, CAR-T therapies can be complicated by life-threatening toxicities such as cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell–associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS), marked by elevated cytokines such as interleukin-1 (IL-1), IL-6, and interferon gamma.4,5 Although immunosuppressive agents such steroids and tocilizumab, an anti–IL-6 receptor antibody, can reverse these toxicities, early use of these agents had been thought to be detrimental to the expansion and tumor-killing effects of CAR-T immunotherapy.6

Subsequent arms of ZUMA-1 trial explored the impact of earlier steroid and tocilizumab intervention on toxicity outcomes. Cohort 3 of ZUMA-1 evaluated the impact of levetiracetam on day 0 and prophylactic tocilizumab on day 2 and found decreased rates of severe (grade 3+) CRS but not ICANS.7 Cohort 4 intervened even earlier than the registrational cohort 1/2 trials, with tocilizumab and steroids use for grade 1 CRS if no improvement was observed within 3 days.8 Steroids were also used for grade 1 ICANS in cohort 4. With a follow-up of 14.8 months, the cohort 4 trial found decreased rates of severe CRS and ICANS and lower cumulative dose of steroid use, with no difference in CRRs vs the ZUMA-1 cohort 1 study.8

The COVID-19 pandemic brought unprecedented challenges to CAR-T toxicity management. Increased strains on the health care system necessitated interventions to keep patients out of limited intensive care unit (ICU) space.9 Nationwide drug shortages, such as tocilizumab, also motivated the need for alternative regimens for CAR-T lymphodepletion and toxicity management.10 In response to these challenges, our center adopted a modified protocol from ZUMA-1 cohort 4 for CAR-T toxicity management in July 2020. Our center initiated steroid therapy for grade 1 CRS and ICANS when symptoms persisted beyond 24 hours, earlier than the 72-hour threshold used in cohort 4. To conserve the limited supply of tocilizumab (Figure 1), we incorporated anakinra, an IL-1 receptor antagonist with superior blood-brain barrier penetration than tocilizumab, into our CRS/ICANS management strategy.11 IL-1 inhibition has been shown to decrease both CRS and neurotoxicity in multiple preclinical studies at comparable or more potent levels than IL-6 inhibition, which was corroborated by case reports that demonstrated anakinra as an effective adjunct to tocilizumab for CAR-T toxicity management.12, 13, 14 Therefore, we used anakinra for recurrent grade CRS/ICANS after an initial dose of tocilizumab.Figure 1.
Comparison of ZUMA-1 cohort 4 vs Stanford protocol.

In this study, we set out to understand the impact of this toxicity management change in patients treated with axi-cel for R/R LBCL at our institution in the third-line (3L+) setting. Here, we compare the pharmacological utilization, toxicity incidence/duration, efficacy, health care utilization, and CAR-T expansion kinetics before and after the toxicity management change.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This is a single-center, retrospective real-world study.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: Patients receiving axi-cel therapy between January 2018 and April 2023 for R/R LBCL with ≥2 prior lines of therapy were included. We excluded patients treated with axi-cel in the second-line setting due to inherent differences in treatment indications and clinical context compared to those receiving therapy in the 3L+ setting. Furthermore, the US Food and Drug Administration approval of axi-cel in the second-line setting via the ZUMA-7 trial occurred after our institution’s protocol change in July 2020, introducing a temporal imbalance that serves as a confounder not easily addressed by statistical modeling.15 This discrepancy reflects differences in treatment era, including evolving supportive care practices, variations in bridging therapy, and broader shifts in clinical management over time. Patients who received axi-cel infusion before 1 July 2020 (the date of toxicity management protocol change) were labeled as the comparator cohort, and those after were labeled as the postchange cohort. A 2-week buffer period before and after 1 July 2020 was implemented to allow for the protocol change to take effect.

sec.title: Data collection
sec.p: Baseline and clinical characteristics were collected retrospectively via electronic chart review. Glucocorticoid, anakinra, and tocilizumab administration 1 month after axi-cel infusion were collected by chart review of the inpatient electronic medical record and stored in a secure database. Steroid use was converted to dexamethasone equivalents, and for patients discharged on steroids, we assumed full adherence to their prescribed outpatient course. CAR-HEMATOTOX score was used to assess hematotoxicity risk.16

CRS and ICANS were defined by the American Society for Transplantation and Cell Therapy criteria.17 Length of hospitalization was defined as the time from admission for CAR-T infusion to hospital discharge. Toxicity time to onset was defined from infusion date to the date of initial presentation of toxicities. Length of toxicity was defined from the date of initial toxicity presentation to the date of resolution.

Overall response rate (ORR) was defined as the proportion of patients who had a partial response or CR to treatment. CRR was defined as the proportion of patients who only had CR to treatment. Disease progression was determined based on clinical judgment by the primary treating physician based on unequivocal clinical, radiologic, or pathologic evidence of lymphoma progression. Time to progression was defined from infusion date to the date of progressive disease, and time to death was defined from infusion date to the date of death. The time of last contact was recorded as the most recent health care interaction documented in the electronic medical records (EMR).
The follow-up cutoff date was 30 June 2024.

sec.title: Sample collection and flow cytometry analysis
sec.p: CAR-T expansion was measured by real-time flow cytometry with anti-idiotype FMC63 conjugated to DyLight 650.18,19 The expansion of CAR T cells was calculated by taking the log10-transformed sum of the absolute values of CD4 and CD8 CAR T cells at days +7 and +14 after infusion. The linear trapezoidal method was used to calculate the area under the curve (AUC) of CAR T-cell expansion for the first 28 days after CAR-T infusion. AUCs were calculated for the CD4 and CD8 components, combined using raw values, with the results then being transformed using a log base-10 transformation. Patients were required to have 3 time points for an accurate AUC to be calculated: both time points surrounding peak expansion (days 7 and 14) and at least 1 time point after peak expansion (days 21 or 28). Infection data were collected from 14 days to 365 days after CAR-T, and infection severity was graded based on Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Continuous variables were presented as medians and interquartile ranges (IQRs) and compared using Mann-Whitney U test, whereas categorical variables were presented as counts and percentages and compared using χ2 tests (or Fisher exact tests, when applicable).

The reverse Kaplan-Meier method was used to estimate median follow-up.20 The Kaplan-Meier method was used to plot estimated survival probabilities against time for progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) outcomes, whereas the cumulative intensity was plotted for the time to first dose outcomes.

Multivariable regression models were fit for the outcomes of interest and the main predictor of toxicity management protocol. Additional covariates, including age, sex, prior stem cell transplant, prelymphodepletion lactate dehydrogenase, bridging therapy before CAR-T infusion, baseline metabolic tumor volume, and CAR-HEMATOTOX, were included as potential confounders.
Statistical significance was determined at the P value <.05 level. All analyses were conducted in R (v 4.3.1).
The research was approved by the institutional review board, and all patients provided written consent before data collection.

sec.title: Results
sec.p:
Between January 2018 and April 2023, a total of 195 patients received axi-cel for R/R LBCL as the third or later line of therapy. Of these, 92 patients were in the comparator cohort (received CAR-T before 1 July 2020), and 103 patients were in the postchange cohort (received CAR-T after 1 July 2020). The median patient age was 63 years (IQR, 55-71), and 83 patients (42.6%) were female. The 3 most common LBCL types were diffuse LBCL (53.3%), transformed follicular lymphoma (19.5%), and high-grade B-cell lymphoma (16.4%). The median number of prior therapies was 3 (IQR, 2-4). The comparator cohort had a higher proportion of patients with high CAR-HEMATOTOX toxicity risk score (51.1% vs 34.0%; P = .035), suggestive of a higher risk of neutropenia.16 Other baseline characteristics were similar between the 2 cohorts (Table 1). The median follow-up time was 40 months (IQR, 29-56).

Pharmacological utilization patterns demonstrated that the new toxicity management protocol was implemented as planned. Patients received steroids earlier in their CAR-T toxicity course, with the comparator group receiving steroids at 7 days (95% confidence interval [CI], 6-8) and the postchange group receiving steroids at 5 days (95% CI, 5-5; Figure 2A). The postchange cohort had a higher incidence of anakinra (22% vs 5%) and steroid use (88% vs 71%) than the comparator cohort, with an adjusted odds ratio (OR) of 6.28 (95% CI, 2.07-24.76; P = .003) for anakinra and 3.90 (95% CI, 1.64-10.05; P = .003) for steroids (Figure 2A-B). There was no significant difference in tocilizumab usage rate (adj. OR, 1.17; 95% CI, 0.56-2.45; P = .681). Steroid and tocilizumab use rates did not vary based on toxicity severity (supplemental Figure 1A). Cumulative dosage of steroids, anakinra, and tocilizumab were not different between the 2 groups (Figure 2B). ICANS severity did not affect cumulative steroid dose (supplemental Figure 1B-C).Figure 2.
Pharmacological interventions in comparator vs postchange cohorts. (A) Cumulative incidence plots of anakinra, steroid, and tocilizumab use in the comparator (n = 92) and postchange cohorts (n = 103). (B) Use rates and cumulative doses of anakinra, steroid, and tocilizumab between postchange vs comparator cohorts. Adjusted analyses included additional covariates of age, sex, bridging treatment, prelymphodepletion lactate dehydrogenase, prior autologous stem cell transplantation, baseline metabolic tumor volume, and HEMATOTOX score categorization (high vs low).

The incidence of toxicity events was similar after the protocol modification, with near identical rates of patients experiencing CRS (93% comparator vs 92% postchange; adj P = .982) and ICANS (51% comparator vs 46% postchange; adj P = .733). The rates of severe (grade 3+) CRS were directionally lower in the postchange group (2% comparator vs 1% postchange; P = not reached). Severe ICANS rates were directionally lower in the postchange cohort (12% vs 21% [comparator]) but did not reach the level of significance (adj. hazard ratio [HR], 0.60; 95% CI, 0.20-1.76; P = .36). There were also no observed differences in the time to onset of CRS or ICANS overall or when split by severity (supplemental Figure 2A-B).

Despite no changes in incidence or toxicity onset, more patients in the postchange cohort experienced earlier resolution of CRS/ICANS (Figure 3). The time from toxicity onset to peak toxicity was shorter in the postchange cohort for both CRS (adj. HR, 1.91; 95% CI, 1.36-2.68; P = .0002; Figure 3A) and ICANS events (adj. HR, 2.20; 95% CI, 1.32-3.66; P = .0025; Figure 3B). Furthermore, there was a difference in the duration of CRS and ICANS events between the 2 cohorts (Figure 3C). The postchange cohort had a shorter CRS duration than the comparator cohort (unadjusted est, ˗1.00 days [95% CI, ˗1.71 to ˗0.30]; adj. est, ˗0.93 days [95% CI, ˗1.67 to ˗0.19]; P = .01; Figure 3A). The duration of ICANS events was also shorter in the postchange cohort (unadjusted est, ˗2.96 days [95% CI, ˗5.18 to ˗0.73]; adj. est, ˗2.49 days [95% CI, ˗4.96 to ˗0.03]; P = .05; Figure 3B). Differences in toxicity duration were also observed when stratified by ICANS severity (supplemental Figure 2C).Figure 3.
CRS/ICANS duration before and after toxicity management change. (A) Length of CRS for comparator (n = 92) vs postchange cohorts (n = 103), demonstrating 0.9 days shorter CRS duration (adjusted P = .01) and earlier toxicity peak in the postchange cohort (time from CRS onset to Max (maximum toxicity), 1.5 vs 0 days; adj P < .01). All grade (92% vs 93%; P = .98) and severe (grade 3+) CRS incidence are directionally lower in the postchange cohort (1% vs 2%; P = not reached). (B) Length of ICANS for comparator vs postchange cohort patients demonstrating 2.5 days shorter ICANS duration (adjusted P = .05) and earlier toxicity peak in the postchange cohort (time from ICANS onset to Max, 2 vs 0 days; adj P < .01). All grade (46% vs 51%; P = .73) and severe (grade 3+) ICANS incidence are directionally lower in the postchange cohort (12% vs 21%; P = .36). (C) Duration (measured in days) of CRS and ICANS toxicity experienced by the comparator vs postchange cohorts.

Best clinical response was similar between the comparator and postchange cohorts (Figure 4A), with no differences observed in CRR (adj. OR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.33-1.55; P = .41) or ORR (adj. OR, 0.83; 95% CI, 0.31-2.18; P = .71). Similarly, 12-month PFS (adj. HR, 0.91; 95% CI, 0.60-1.39; P = .67) and OS (adj. HR, 1.10; 95% CI, 0.68-1.79; P = .70) were similar across the 2 cohorts (Figure 4B).Figure 4.
Clinical response and survival. (A) Distribution of treatment response, in which ORR = CR + partial response. (B) PFS and OS curves between the comparator and postchange cohorts. PD, progressive disease; SD, stable disease.

Regarding infections, the postchange cohort had a lower rate of patients experiencing infections of any grade (54% vs 77%; adj. OR, 0.44 [95% CI, 0.21-0.87]; P = .02) and a directionally lower rate of those experiencing severe (Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events grade 3+) infections (26% vs 39%; adj. OR, 0.65 [95% CI, 0.32-1.29]; P = .22).

Health care utilization, defined by ICU admission rates and hospitalization duration, was also similar between the comparator and postchange cohorts. The postchange cohort had directionally lower ICU admission rates (9% vs 11%; P = .70) and hospitalization duration (median, 12 vs 13 days; P = .18), without reaching statistical significance.

CAR-T expansion data, measured by flow cytometry, showed lower expansion in the postchange cohort. Expansion at day 7 was lower in the postchange cohort (adj. est, ˗0.46 log10-units; 95% CI, ˗0.89 to ˗0.03; P = .04) but not significantly lower at day 14 (adj. est, ˗0.15 log10-units; 95% CI, ˗0.47 to 0.17; P = .35; Figure 5A). Total CAR-T expansion, as measured by AUC, was lower in the postchange cohort (adj. est, ˗0.45 log10-units; 95% CI, ˗0.82 to ˗0.07; P = .02; Figure 5B). However, peak expansion (defined as the highest CAR-T expansion at day 7 or 14) was not significantly different between the postchange and comparator cohorts (adj. est, ˗0.19 log10-units; 95% CI, ˗0.50 to 0.11; P = .22).Figure 5.
CAR-T expansion in the comparator vs postchange cohorts. (A) CAR-T counts (units = cells per microliter) by flow cytometry at days 7 and 14 after axi-cel infusion. (B) Total CAR-T expansion, as measured by AUC. (C) Differences in CAR-T kinetics (CARFACS) between the comparator vs postchange cohorts.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this single-center retrospective study, we found that implementing an early-intervention toxicity management protocol, modeled after ZUMA-1 cohort 4 but incorporating IL-1 blockade with anakinra, significantly improved toxicity outcomes in patients. The modified strategy led to faster resolution of CRS and ICANS events and meaningfully shorter durations of CRS and ICANS (∼1.0 and 2.5 days shorter, respectively) without compromising ORRs, survival outcomes, or health care utilization. Furthermore, the protocol resulted in lower rates of infection within 1 year of treatment (54% vs 77%) and directionally lower rates of severe infection (26% vs 39%). These findings underscore the clinical relevance of our approach. Patients experienced faster resolution of life-threatening toxicities without any loss of CAR-T efficacy, an outcome that validates the safety of earlier corticosteroid use and positions anakinra as a viable adjunct to tocilizumab in CAR-T toxicity management. The ZUMA-1 cohort 4 regimen adopts a conservative, stepwise escalation strategy in which corticosteroids are introduced first for CRS/ICANS, with cytokine blockade typically delayed until ≥3 days of nonresponse. In contrast, the Stanford protocol uses an earlier and more aggressive intervention paradigm, incorporating corticosteroids in combination with up-front or rapidly sequential tocilizumab and, when indicated, anakinra, to intensify cytokine modulation and neurotoxicity prophylaxis. This reflects a shift from delayed, single-agent immunosuppression toward early, multiagent immune blockade to mitigate severe inflammatory toxicities without compromising CAR T-cell efficacy.

Baseline characteristics were largely balanced between the prechange and postchange cohorts, minimizing the potential for confounding. One noted difference was a higher median CAR-HEMATOTOX risk score in the comparator group, indicating greater expected hematologic toxicity risk in that cohort. We adjusted our analyses for this factor and other potential covariates (eg, age, prior transplant, and tumor burden) to ensure the observed benefits of the new protocol were not simply due to baseline differences. Thus, the improvements in toxicity duration and severity can be attributed to the management changes rather than patient-related characteristics.

An initial step in our analysis was confirming that the modified protocol was implemented as intended. Indeed, the post–July 2020 cohort had significantly higher use of steroids (88% vs 71% of patients) and anakinra (22% vs 5%), with a shorter time to first dose for both agents, reflecting adherence to our early intervention protocol. Importantly, this more aggressive up-front approach did not increase overall corticosteroid exposure, with equivalent cumulative steroid dose between cohorts. This finding is reassuring as evidence of better toxicity control without subjecting patients to additional steroid-associated long-term toxicities (eg, opportunistic infections and metabolic complications).21 Although previous comparisons of ZUMA-1 cohort 4 to the original protocol reported a lower total steroid use with earlier intervention, our prechange vs postchange steroid totals were similar.8,22 Finally, tocilizumab use remained unchanged between the cohorts, because our algorithm still used 1 dose of tocilizumab for initial CRS management before switching to anakinra for subsequent cytokine elevations.

Consistent with expectation, the incidence and time to onset of CRS or ICANS events did not differ between the 2 cohorts. This is unsurprising given the similar patient profiles and the fact that our intervention involved early treatment of toxicity rather than prophylactic measures against toxicity onset itself. In other words, implementing earlier steroids and anakinra interventions would not be expected to prevent CRS/ICANS from occurring in a susceptible patient; instead, the benefit lies in mitigating the severity and duration of those events once they begin. Consistent with this, we observed a trend toward lower rates of severe (grade 3+) toxicities in the postchange group, although the difference did not reach statistical significance. Severe CRS occurred in 1% of patients with the new protocol vs 2% before, as well as severe ICANS in 12% vs 21%, respectively. Although our sample size may have limited the power to detect a statistically significant difference, the reduction in severe ICANS (a 43% decrease) is clinically notable. This observation aligns with prior studies suggesting that prompt immunosuppressive intervention can curtail neurotoxicity escalation. For example, the ZUMA-1 cohort 4 trial and subsequent analyses showed markedly lower rates of severe neurologic events when early steroids and tocilizumab were used.8 Similarly, a recent prospective trial of prophylactic anakinra supported the role of IL-1 blockade in mitigating neurotoxicity, reporting a severe ICANS frequency <10%, far below historical rates.23 Taken together, our data and these literature reports reinforce that earlier intervention with steroids and cytokine inhibition has tangible benefits in reducing the most life-threatening forms of CRS/ICANS.

One of our most compelling findings is the significant shortening of CRS/ICANS duration with the modified protocol. On average, CRS resolved ∼1 day faster and ICANS 2.5 days faster in the postchange cohort. Even modest reductions in toxicity duration are meaningful in the CAR-T setting, especially for ICANS events, in which each additional day of encephalopathy or delirium poses risks of injury, prolonged ICU care, and patient distress. A 2.5-day reduction in neurotoxicity duration represents a substantial improvement over current standard management. Furthermore, the time from CRS/ICANS onset to peak CRS/ICANS toxicity was also shorter in the postchange cohort, demonstrating that the new protocol led to faster resolution of toxicities as intended.

Mechanistically, the more pronounced impact on ICANS duration may be explained by the introduction of anakinra. IL-1 is thought to be a key mediator of ICANS pathogenesis, and unlike IL-6, IL-1 and its receptor antagonist cross the blood-brain barrier more readily.4 By blocking IL-1 early in the course of neurologic symptoms, we likely achieved faster abatement of neuroinflammation, consistent with both our clinical data and prior preclinical models. Thus, the combination of earlier corticosteroids with IL-1 receptor blockade appears particularly effective for neurotoxicity management, addressing a major challenge in CAR-T therapy.

Crucially, our augmented toxicity management did not compromise the antitumor efficacy of axi-cel. We observed no significant differences in ORR, PFS, or OS between the 2 cohorts. This mirrors findings from ZUMA-1 cohort 4 and other series that earlier immunosuppressive interventions do not diminish CAR-T effectiveness. Notably, initial concerns that steroids or cytokine blockers could hinder CAR T-cell expansion and curtail therapeutic potency have not borne out in clinical trials, and our real-world data add further reassurance on this point.7,8,24,25 Moreover, earlier steroid intervention did not result in higher rates of infection; to the contrary, the postchange cohort experienced significantly lower rates of any infection and directionally lower rates of severe infection within 1 year of CAR-T infusion. We also saw similar (in fact, nominally lower) rates of ICU admission and length of hospitalization in the postchange group, suggesting that better toxicity control may translate into reduced critical care needs, although our study was not powered to conclusively demonstrate differences in health care utilization. At minimum, the lack of an increase in ICU/hospitalization metrics indicates that the new protocol is not causing any excess morbidity that would necessitate more intensive care. Although different institutions might have varied attitudes toward anakinra use given financial access considerations, potential reductions in health care utilization, improvements in CRS/ICANS duration, and lower infection rates may tilt the calculus toward using anakinra even with the additional costs associated with its use. Future cost-effectiveness analyses can also more fully define the value of this approach.

Our exploration of CAR T-cell kinetics offers additional insight into why early steroid use did not ultimately impair efficacy. We noted that on day 7 after infusion, CAR T-cell expansion (by flow cytometry) was lower in the postchange cohort, and the cumulative expansion AUC over 28 days was correspondingly reduced. This suggests that early corticosteroid administration may transiently temper the initial proliferation of CAR T cells. However, by day 14 and for peak expansion, there were no differences between the cohorts. The early growth delay appears to be rapidly compensated, such that the modified immune effector cells still achieve equivalent peak levels. Biologically, this makes sense: once the initial cytokine surge is blunted and steroids are tapered, CAR T cells can continue to expand. The fact that we observed no difference in clinical outcomes further confirms that any early kinetic differences were negligible in the long run. Because not all patients had serial CAR-T levels measured (∼45%-50% in each cohort), these kinetic conclusions should be interpreted with some caution. Nonetheless, our data indicate that earlier steroid intervention may delay CAR T-cell expansion but does not diminish the overall expansion or effectiveness by day 14 and beyond, a critical distinction for addressing safety without sacrificing efficacy.

There are several limitations to consider. First, the study’s single-center, retrospective design limits generalizability and cannot prove causality. The protocol change was enacted in response to real-world pressures (the COVID-19 pandemic and drug shortages) rather than a randomized trial; therefore, it coincided with temporal factors that are difficult to fully control. For instance, evolving supportive care practices or increasing care experience over time could independently influence toxicity outcomes. We mitigated some bias by adjusting for measurable baseline differences and using consistent grading criteria, but unmeasured confounders may remain. Second, although our cohort of 195 patients is sizeable for a CAR-T study, it may still be underpowered for detecting infrequent events (eg, very rare severe CRS) or subtle differences in outcomes such as long-term survival. Some of the favorable trends (such as reduced ICU use or severe toxicity rates) did not reach statistical significance, and a larger multicenter sample might be needed to confirm those benefits. Third, our toxicity management algorithm, early dexamethasone and anakinra after 1 dose of tocilizumab, was influenced by a tocilizumab shortage and local practice; other centers might use different thresholds or sequence of agents. Whether our results would be replicated in settings without drug scarcity or with other CAR-T products (eg, tisagenlecleucel or lisocabtagene maraleucel, which have different toxicity profiles) is not certain. Thus, caution is warranted in extrapolating our findings beyond axi-cel in the R/R LBCL population. Finally, we did not systematically compare our modified protocol against alternative emerging strategies (such as prophylactic tocilizumab or prophylactic anakinra administration) in this study. Future research could address these comparisons directly.

Despite these limitations, our findings have clear implications for clinical practice and future research. We demonstrate that proactive toxicity management, treating CRS and ICANS early and aggressively, can reduce the morbidity of CAR-T therapy without impeding its efficacy. This has practical significance for CAR-T centers: earlier intervention (including corticosteroids, historically approached cautiously) should be considered when managing persistent low-grade toxicities. The incorporation of anakinra as an IL-1 blocking agent provides an additional tool, especially in cases in which IL-6 blockade alone is insufficient or contraindicated. Our real-world evidence supports recent paradigm shifts in toxicity management, echoing the outcomes of trials such as ZUMA-1 cohort 4 and emerging IL-1 blockade studies.23 We believe these data can inform refinements in institutional protocols and consensus guidelines, encouraging a more aggressive yet safe approach to CRS/ICANS. Prospective trials are warranted to validate our observations and to optimize early intervention strategies further; for example, testing prophylactic anakinra or earlier steroid triggers in a controlled fashion.23 Such studies will be vital to generalize our approach across multiple centers and CAR-T products, ultimately improving the tolerability of CAR-T. In conclusion, early steroid and anakinra use in axi-cel therapy in 3L+ LBCL treatment substantially shortened toxicity durations while maintaining disease control. This novel management approach enhances patient safety and comfort during CAR-T and can serve as a model for enhancing the therapeutic index of cellular immunotherapies.
